guide.heading: Reading the catalogue
guide.text: Use the two sheets together. Filter Evidence by the stable claim ID to see the printed target, the test or example, its provenance and the inference it licenses. Quotation marks in the passage column mark short excerpts. Other descriptions of CGEL there are paraphrases.

guide.heading: Selection and scope
guide.text: The audit reviewed all 20 numbered sections of Chapter 5. Three cross-chapter follow-ups (CG-0058–0060) test claims from Chapters 14 and 19 against other passages and usage data. The catalogue includes positive controls and known errata. Its proportions cannot estimate a chapter-wide error rate. CG-0063–0105 come from a section-by-section error sweep on 19 November 2026. CG-0103–0104 correct references to Chapter 5 printed in Chapters 6 and 15. CG-0106–0111 test lexical claims against the Oxford English Dictionary.

guide.heading: Editorial assessments
guide.text: Correction proposes changing a particular claim. Qualification narrows its scope or evidential force. Argument gap identifies an inference the evidence fails to establish. Textual mismatch records incompatible wording or labels across passages. Extension supplies an account or test beyond the description. Production error records a misprint, a wrong cross-reference or a misnumbered example that the authors’ errata do not list. Pages refer to the corrected printing used for the audit.

guide.heading: Evidence and provenance
guide.text: Supported means that the tested distinction survives the stated challenge. Open means that live alternatives remain. Author erratum identifies a correction by the authors. These filters answer different questions and have no numerical order. Not yet reviewed (the Author review column, and a label on the website) marks an entry drafted with AI assistance that the author hasn’t yet checked.

guide.heading: Semantic inference
guide.text: Yes marks an argument that depends on a construal, meaning or participant role. Read the inference and finding to see whether the meaning supplies evidence, leaves competitors tied or conflicts with a stated restriction. Both supported and challenged arguments can receive Yes.

guide.heading: Condition under test
guide.text: Necessary asks whether an instance must meet the condition. Sufficient asks whether meeting it establishes the analysis. Distributional restriction concerns permitted forms or environments. Diagnostic only concerns the weight of a clue. A distributional rule or diagnostic can also have logical force. The field gives the aspect tested in this row. None means no such condition was singled out.

guide.heading: Internal tension
guide.text: Yes flags passages to compare. Their bearing can differ: the PP in CG-0026 receives two function labels, premises in CG-0039/0047 partly rely on one another, and CG-0049 invites a comparison of evidential standards. A double-standard claim needs comparable inferences and controls for independent structural evidence.

guide.heading: Argument families
guide.text: CG-0004/0005 test opposite directions of an individuation claim. CG-0019/0020 distinguish available alternatives from realized variation. CG-0039 and CG-0047–0049 concern intertwined premises about nominal arguments and subjects. Treat each group as related evidence when discussing the findings.

guide.heading: How to weigh a source
guide.text: A constructed contrast tests a prediction. An attestation establishes a use in that source. Its date and register bound historical and variety claims. A research source may supply data or a rival analysis. A related manuscript records intellectual context. An access copy is another route to the same work. Working-note rows give the argument in the sheet itself.

claims.claim: CGEL limits nominal by-obliques to agents and uses that limit in its argument against voice in NPs.
claims.evidence_summary: Bruening’s receipt example makes Gift Processing the recipient of a form. In the advance-knowledge example the investors are the people who knew about the attacks. The latter state can hold without the investors doing anything. Neither by-phrase gives a place, instrument or time.
claims.finding: The examples defeat the agent-only premise in reason (c). Reasons (a) and (b) still stand: nominal forms lack the active/passive contrast, and a single nominal can express both participants as obliques. These data alone do not decide nominal voice.
claims.proposed_wording: The nominal head constrains which participant can be expressed in a by-phrase. Attested possibilities include the agent of a conquest, the recipient in a receipt event, the experiencer of a perception, and the holder of knowledge.
claims.traditional_parallel: Pp. 227–228 separate subject function from typical agenthood. P. 476 uses an agent-only contrast as one argument about nominal voice. Bruening removes that empirical contrast. Showing a double standard would also require holding the competing structural diagnostics constant.
claims.inference: Must the by-phrase of an event or state nominal denote an agent?

evidence.source: Benjamin Bruening (2013). By phrases in passives and nominals. Syntax 16(1), 1–41.

evidence.example: In (23) an office receives the form. In (25) investors have advance knowledge of attacks. In (21b) the by-phrase also follows the of-phrase, matching the order in CGEL’s starred knowledge example.
evidence.establishes: Recipient and knower are available roles. Reason (c) loses its role contrast. The absence of verbal inflection and the double-oblique pattern remain independent considerations.

claims.claim: After acknowledging varied readings of other nominalizations, CGEL argues that an event noun determines its genitive’s role as firmly as the corresponding verb determines its subject’s, especially where a further complement is overt.
claims.evidence_summary: The mayors’ release dates a signing with today’s, identifies the legislation in an of-phrase and its signer in a by-phrase. Its next sentence explicitly credits Trump with signing. Compare “The president signed the legislation today”. The time is an adjunct in the clause.
claims.finding: Event meaning and an overt theme do not force the external genitive to supply a participant. A distinct position for temporal genitives could explain the example if there is independent evidence for it. Subjecthood for personal genitives remains open.
claims.proposed_wording: An event noun with an overt theme readily permits a participant interpretation for a personal genitive. An external genitive can also locate the event in time, including when both agent and theme are independently expressed.
claims.inference: Does an overt theme force the initial genitive of an event nominal to express a participant?

evidence.source: U.S. Conference of Mayors (29 January 2020). Statement by U.S. Conference of Mayors President on Signing of USMCA Legislation.
evidence.passage: §16.5.2, p. 475, paragraph after [55ib], Ed’s destruction of the file. CGEL calls a different role “hardly possible”, especially with a further complement, and concludes that noun and verb determine the role “to the same extent”. Compare p. 474 [54xvii].
evidence.example: The release says “today's signing of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) implementation legislation by President Trump”. The next sentence names Trump as the person who signed it.
evidence.establishes: The genitive dates the event while both participants are overt. A temporal adjunct expresses its contribution in the corresponding clause. The token leaves the syntax of personal genitives open.

claims.claim: A count noun denotes individuals which cannot divide into smaller things of the same kind.
claims.evidence_summary: “We divided an interval into three shorter intervals” (constructed). The article an and the numeral three with a plural independently mark the two count uses. The original interval and each of its three proper parts satisfy the same noun in the same mathematical sense.
claims.finding: Counting requires a unit at the chosen level of description. It does not require a unit with no interval as a proper part. Conversely, people may count pieces to judge how much furniture there is (CG-0005).
claims.proposed_wording: A count use presents entities as units relative to a context. An interval may count as one unit even when it contains shorter intervals. Use the distribution with numerals and determiners to identify count syntax.
claims.inference: Must a count individual lack proper parts that also satisfy the same noun?

evidence.source: OpenStax, Calculus Volume 2. Chapter 1, Key Terms.
evidence.passage: §3.1, p. 335, paragraph after [5]. Having defined a count use through individuals and illustrated boy, CGEL says they “cannot be divided into smaller parts of the same kind as the whole”.
evidence.example: A partition divides an interval into subintervals. Each subinterval is an interval in the same mathematical sense. The example with an and three shorter intervals is constructed in this audit.
evidence.establishes: The source establishes the part–whole relation. In the constructed sentence the article and the low cardinal independently establish the count distribution.
evidence.locator: Entries for partition and regular partition.

claims.claim: CGEL infers that the universal component of free choice is implicated from the fact that an instruction to take either computer need not instruct the addressee to take both.
claims.evidence_summary: Fix two laptops, one blue and one silver. “You may take either, but not both” leaves both individual options open. “You may take either, but you may not take the blue one” withdraws one of those options. Both continuations are constructed.
claims.finding: Permission to select blue and permission to select silver can coexist with a prohibition on taking the pair. The imperative tests joint selection. It leaves open whether the availability of each single option is entailed or implicated.
claims.proposed_wording: An instruction to take either computer makes each computer available for selection and commonly licenses taking only one. Whether the availability of each alternative is entailed or implicated requires a test that keeps the number selected constant.
claims.inference: Does withholding permission to take two items jointly withdraw permission for either single choice?

evidence.source: Maria Aloni (2007). Free choice, modals, and imperatives. Natural Language Semantics 15(1), 65–94. DOI 10.1007/s11050-007-9010-2.
evidence.passage: §5.1, pp. 361–362. Compare suitability in [11b], permission in [12], and the imperative argument immediately following. Its pivot is “not an instruction to take all or both of them”.
evidence.example: Being free to choose any single key differs from being instructed to press every key. The laptop continuations in the audit are constructed.
evidence.establishes: Prior analysis supplies an analogous contrast. The laptop test isolates what CGEL’s inference would have to establish.
evidence.locator: P. 66, examples (1)–(4), particularly the instruction about keys in (3).

claims.claim: In §19.2, with semantically plural predicands in ascriptive constructions lacking explicit quantification, rule [12] assigns non-distributive interpretation to singular predicatives.
claims.evidence_summary: “Coin envelopes are a good size for most seeds” describes the individual envelopes. Give a seedling a 10-cm pot and a tree a 40-cm pot. “The pots are a suitable size for their respective plants” can be true. In that context the unmarked “These pots are a suitable size” can also be true, then false after swapping the plants.
claims.finding: Suitability applies separately to each pot although the predicative NP is singular and their sizes differ. A single shared value is possible but unnecessary. The argument against general grammatical number concord survives.
claims.proposed_wording: With a semantically plural predicand, a singular predicative may attribute a property to the group or to each member. In the latter case each member may satisfy the description with a different value.
claims.inference: Does a singular count predicative force the property to apply to the bearers collectively?

evidence.source: Mikaela Boley (2020). Collecting Native Seed. University of Maryland Extension.
evidence.passage: §19.2, p. 513, [12], following [11i–ii]. The rule assigns plural forms distributively and “singular forms non-distributively”. Its domain excludes specifying predicatives and explicit quantification. The quantified cases are taken up on p. 515.
evidence.example: “Coin envelopes are a good size for most seeds.” The advice concerns which individual envelopes can hold the material. The dimensions of a stack would not answer that question.
evidence.establishes: A singular predicative is applicable to individual bearers. The different-sized pots in the audit test the further suggestion that those bearers have to share one value.
evidence.locator: Handout p. 9, Taking Care of Collected Seed, first bullet.

claims.claim: Enough does not modify the core degree determinatives: enough money (or money enough), not ∗much enough money.
claims.evidence_summary: OED quotations with sufficiency enough after few: For a relatively short accelerator, there may be few enough grids so that a considerable fraction of the ion beam penetrates all the grids (J. C. Slater, Microwave Electronics, 1950, under grid, n.¹); A number of persons who communicate with one another often over a span of time, and..few enough so that each person is able to communicate with all the others..face-to-face (G. C. Homans, Human Group, 1950, under primary group, n.). Every little enough found in determiner function has the understatement sense “very little”: There was little enough comfort for us subalterns (A. Griffiths, 1904); Little enough encouragement was there (Lancet, 1946); have little enough money left for reinvestment except in technology (C. Coker, Humane Warfare, 2001). Few enough men and scarcely any women can tell the difference (Illustrated American, 1893) is the same use. OED quotation searches find no many enough, and one much enough, a 1562 proverb about the word itself: This woord enough twoo waies we may skan. Thone much enough, thother littell enough (J. Heywood).
claims.finding: Sufficiency enough modifies few, in determiner function in Slater and also in Homans, where a group is defined by its size; the restriction fails for few. A defender could read Slater as understatement followed by a separate result clause, but that reading doesn’t fit Homans’s definition. The evidence is two quotations, both from 1950. CGEL doesn’t define “core”, but §7.11 and §11(c) (p. 431) both name many, much, few and little. No sufficiency little enough in determiner function was found: those quotations are the understatement use. The OED (enough, revised 2020) separates an intensive adverb sense (“fully, quite, pretty, very”) from “Sufficiently” but doesn’t place little enough in either, so treating it as the intensive use is an inference. For much and many the OED quotations agree with CGEL: many enough has no hits, and the one much enough is a 1562 proverb about the word enough.
claims.proposed_wording: Note, however, that in this sense it doesn’t modify much, many or little: we have enough money (or money enough), not ∗much enough money. It can modify few: there may be few enough grids so that a considerable fraction of the ion beam penetrates all the grids. Little enough in determiner function has the understatement sense “very little” (There was little enough comfort for us subalterns).
claims.inference: Does sufficiency enough combine with any core degree determinative?

claims.topic: The plague with and without the article
claims.claim: Some common infectious diseases optionally take the definite article ((the) flu, (the) measles). With the plague, the article is obligatory.
claims.evidence_summary: OED plague, n. sense 3c, the disease caused by Yersinia pestis: “Frequently in the plague.” Bare plague occurs in its quotations, e.g. during the prevalence of plague (E. W. Lane, 1841). The WHO fact sheet has Plague is an infectious disease and effective against plague. In the have frame, the OED’s one example keeps the article: suspected of having the plague (Times, 1994).
claims.finding: The article is frequent, not obligatory, with this noun. The claim may hold for the have frame of [17iii], which none of the sources tests with a bare noun.
claims.proposed_wording: With plague, the article is usual, especially after have: He has the plague.
claims.inference: Does the disease noun plague require the definite article?

evidence.example: Sense 3c: “Frequently in the plague.” 1841 Some Muslims even shut themselves up during the prevalence of plague (Lane). 1994 eight people suspected of having the plague (Times).
evidence.establishes: An edited dictionary treats the article as frequent rather than required. The have-frame example has the article.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, sense 3c. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.

evidence.source: World Health Organization, Plague fact sheet.
evidence.example: “Plague is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis”; “Antibiotics and supportive therapy are effective against plague”.
evidence.establishes: Current edited medical prose uses bare plague as subject and as object of a preposition.
evidence.locator: Key facts and treatment sections. Fetched by a reader on 19 November 2026.

claims.topic: At dark as a time of day
claims.claim: Bare NPs for times of day follow at, by, before, until and after, but morning, daytime, evening and dark take in + the instead of at.
claims.evidence_summary: OED quotations with at dark for nightfall: returned at dark with only five men (D. Haig, diary, 1915); We reached Biela at dark (Daily News, 1877); At dark John Henry came to the back door (C. McCullers, The Member of the Wedding, 1946); at daybreak or at dark (Hunting Annual, 1980).
claims.finding: Dark patterns with night and dawn in taking bare at. In the dark is a locative or state expression rather than a time of day. The claim holds for morning, daytime and evening.
claims.proposed_wording: note, however, that morning, daytime and evening take in + the instead of at: in the / ∗at morning
claims.inference: Does dark, as a time of day, take in the rather than at?

evidence.source: Oxford English Dictionary, quotation search for “at dark”.
evidence.example: 1877 We reached Biela at dark (Daily News, under earth-coloured, adj.). 1915 returned at dark (Haig, under dark, n.). 1946 At dark John Henry came to the back door (McCullers, under weekend, n.). 1980 at daybreak or at dark (Hunting Ann., under owling, n.).
evidence.establishes: At dark for nightfall in edited British and American prose across a century.

claims.claim: Shambles has no plural form: These rooms are a shambles, not ∗These rooms are shambles.
claims.evidence_summary: OED shamble, n.¹ sense 5b, “a scene of disorder or devastation; a ruin; a mess”, originally U.S., from 1926. Every quotation has a shambles or in a shambles. Quotation searches for are shambles and were shambles return nothing.
claims.finding: The lexical premise holds in the OED. The further inference that shambles cannot be used distributively is tested in CG-0053.
claims.inference: Does the disorder sense of shambles have a plural?

evidence.example: Sense 5b, 1926–: became a shambles of cluttered flasks (1926); a thorough shambles (1966); its economy in a shambles (1979).
evidence.establishes: Singular construal with a throughout; no plural attested.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, sense 5b; quotation searches “are shambles”, “were shambles” (0 results). Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.
